title: Performance and the instruction cycle
kicker: ENCT 303 · Computer Organization and Architecture · Chapter 1
subtitle: How to say a computer is “fast” with a number, and what the processor actually does between two ticks.

sections.title: Organisation versus architecture
sections.body:
Computer architecture is what a programmer can see: the instruction set, registers, addressing modes and data types. Computer organisation is how it is built to provide that: control signals, buses, cache design, the technology. Two machines with the same architecture (two x86 chips) can have very different organisations — and different speeds.

A computer is a processor that fetches instructions and data from memory, with I/O to the outside world, joined by a bus. A multi-core processor simply puts several processors on one chip sharing the memory system.

questions.prompt: Two processors run the same programs but one is faster. What differs?

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: A different architecture could not run the same binaries.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The instruction set is identical (that is what “same programs” means); speed comes from pipelines, caches and clock rate.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: The programs are given as identical.

figures.note: The three buses carry addresses, data and control signals.

sections.title: The instruction cycle
sections.body:
Every instruction goes through the same loop: fetch it from the address in the program counter, decode what it asks for, execute it (possibly fetching operands and writing a result), then advance the program counter. A jump simply loads a new address into the counter. Interrupts are checked between instructions.

Watch an Intel 8085 do exactly this: each step is one instruction, the highlighted row is the one about to run, and the registers and flags change beneath.

questions.prompt: After a normal (non-jump) instruction executes, what happens to the program counter?

choices.text: It stays at the same address.
It is advanced to the next instruction (by the instruction’s length).

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: Then the same instruction would run forever.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: A jump, call or return overwrites it; everything else just steps forward, which is why straight-line code runs in order.

figures.caption: Figure 1.2.1 — fetch – decode – execute
figures.note: Adds 25H + 17H: the result 3CH lands in memory at 2052H.

sections.title: Measuring performance
sections.body: Execution time = instruction count × CPI (cycles per instruction) × clock period. The clock rate is only one of the three factors; a faster clock with a worse CPI can be slower. MIPS = instruction count / (time × 10⁶) = clock rate / (CPI × 10⁶), but MIPS misleads across different instruction sets.

worked.why: A 2 GHz processor runs a program of 10⁹ instructions at CPI 1.5.
Cycles = instructions × CPI. Time = cycles / clock.

questions.prompt: A compiler change cuts the instruction count by 20% but raises CPI by 30%. Net effect on time?

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Time scales with the product; a saving in one factor can be eaten by another.

sections.title: Amdahl's law
sections.body: Speeding up only a fraction f of a program by a factor s gives overall speed-up 1 / ((1 − f) + f/s). The serial part (1 − f) caps everything: even with infinite s the limit is 1/(1 − f). This is why adding cores helps a little for mostly-serial programs.

worked.why: A program spends 80% of its time in a part that can be made 4× faster.

questions.prompt: If 10% of a program is serial, the maximum speed-up with unlimited processors is…

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: Confuses the parallel fraction with the speed-up.

problems.prompt: A 500 MHz machine executes 10⁸ instructions with a CPI of 2.5. Execution time?
Half of a program is sped up 10×. Overall speed-up?

sections.title: RISC and CISC
sections.body: CISC machines (x86) have many complex, variable-length instructions, some of which do a lot of work. RISC machines (ARM, RISC-V, MIPS) have few, simple, fixed-length instructions, use load/store for all memory access and keep many registers — which makes pipelining easy. Berkeley RISC added overlapped register windows: each procedure gets a window of registers that overlaps its caller's, so parameters are passed without touching memory.

questions.prompt: Why do RISC processors allow only load/store instructions to touch memory?

choices.text: It keeps every other instruction register-to-register and fixed in duration, which makes pipelining simple.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Uniform timing is the key enabler of a smooth pipeline.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: RISC has more registers, not fewer.

figures.caption: Figure 1.5.1 — RISC vs CISC
figures.note: Complexity lives in microcode (CISC) or in the compiler (RISC).

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
• Architecture = visible contract; organisation = implementation.
  • Time = instructions × CPI × period.
  • Amdahl: the serial fraction limits speed-up.
  • The instruction cycle: fetch, decode, execute, repeat.
